connection_type: I have direct personal experience (as an immigrant, refugee, religious minority, or member of a marginalised group)
disclosure_text: I immigrated from Nigeria to Canada when I was eighteen years old and have lived through various phases of trying to integrate and become established in my new country.
micronarrative:
What stands out to me is how deeply polarizing immigration is, and how blurry the line between right and wrong is when it comes to this issue. The people calling for stricter enforcement at the border are not wrong, and those claiming no one is "illegal" are also not wrong. I felt a similar conflict when I learned that Canadians hold the view that accepting immigrants into the country effectively shrinks the labour market and reduces how many jobs there are for Canadians. On the one hand, I came here to prosper economically, and to do that, I needed to find employment. It was not a choice but a necessity. And I felt I was only allowed to come because the government anticipated that I could become economically prosperous without harming others' prospects. But on the other hand, I felt bad that I was a contributor to these concerns that were being raised, and even empathized with the Canadians because once I understood the reality, I was able to see that their fears were valid.

I definitely adjust my tone depending on who I am speaking to. I sound different—more Nigerian—when speaking to other Nigerians. When speaking to Canadians or in an official capacity at work, I sound more like them. I don't even do it intentionally; it just happens naturally. It happens every day at work, during meetings. Not about immigration, but about general topics. 

I try to stay away from discussing immigration with people of other backgrounds. However, I remember speaking to a coworker about the realities of life back home and how they compare to life here. I spoke about how the hardship people face in my home country forges them into physically and mentally capable individuals, and how that fortitude serves them well in any capacity or setting they find themselves. In that conversation, I relaxed into my natural self, used my natural tone, and did not try to sound any particular way. I was a bit more direct than usual and spoke with a passion I feel like the subject warranted and deserved.

annotations.rationale: The statement, "at some point , we have to describe who this country is actually for" sounds pointed and judgemental towards a minority group. annotations.tweet_text: My grandparents came here legally and waited years. Why should anyone get to skip that line?
annotations.participant_label: Not harmful — policy concern, cultural commentary, or frustration with no hateful subtext
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale: Skipping the line is used here as a metaphor for describing immigrants enjoying the same benefits as those who were born here, paid their dues and their taxes. Indigenes or locals often carry the idea that immigrants must pay a certain due or reach a particular threshold before they should be allowed certain rights or benefits, like access to healthcare or voting.
